narrative.overview: RASAD treats every supply movement the way an IAF air-traffic controller treats a flight: as a paper strip in a bay. A strip has fixed cells (who, how long the stock lasts, the last road day) and a coloured holder that names the transport mode. The commander reads the bay from top to bottom, most urgent first, and stamps the strip to approve it. The world is light and calm, because it is shown on projectors and read by officers who want the decision, not decoration.
keyCharacteristics: Light bay board, paper strips, ink type; no dark command-centre look.
Mode is always icon + word + colour, never colour alone.
Every number carries a unit; every recommendation carries a one-line why and a confidence.
Data provenance shows as small plies: Real (solid ink), Simulated (dashed hatch), PLACEHOLDER (yellow errata slip).

rules.name: The Holder Rule
rules.body: A transport mode is shown in its holder colour together with its icon and its word (Jeep, Mule, Porter, Heli, Drone). Status colours are never used for modes.

rules.name: The Ply Rule
rules.body: Provenance is a ply, not a paragraph: Real is solid ink, Simulated is a dashed hatched ply, PLACEHOLDER is a yellow errata slip. Details live in the chip's popover.

rules.name: The One Family Rule
rules.body: One family (Barlow) at every size; the condensed width is the only change of voice.

dos: Do pair every mode colour with its icon and word.
Do show units on every number and "(80%)" on every confidence-bearing date or band.
Do put cost multiples next to their inputs and a PLACEHOLDER chip.
Do keep text in ink tokens; colour carries identity or status, not sentences.
donts: Don't use camouflage, hacker green, glowing radar or a dark command-centre theme.
Don't show international boundary lines on any map.
Don't reuse status colours (red, amber, green) for transport modes or chart series.
Don't add eyebrow labels above headings or decorate with gradients and glass.
